title: 天順六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
列聖相承莫不以育賢為首務故在唐宋
盛時學制猶有州士不滿二百不得
立學者今則自
京畿以迄四海無地無學即古黨庠
遂序之制矣科目有取辭章對偶至
使豪傑顏忸怩而不屑就者今則學
校既以經術教人科目亦以經術取
士士非詩書禮樂之文不習非堯舜

立學者今則自

校既以經術教人科目亦以經術取
士士非詩書禮樂之文不習非堯舜
punctuated: 列聖相承，莫不以育賢為首務。故在唐宋盛時，學制猶有州士不滿二百不得立學者，今則自京畿以迄四海，無地無學，即古黨庠遂序之制矣。科目有取辭章對偶，至使豪傑顏忸怩而不屑就者，今則學校既以經術教人，科目亦以經術取士。士非詩書禮樂之文不習，非堯舜
translation_en: The successive Sacred Emperors have followed one another, and none failed to take the nurturing of worthies as their foremost duty. Thus, even in the flourishing eras of the Tang and Song dynasties, the school system still had regulations whereby prefectures with fewer than two hundred scholars were not permitted to establish a school; today, however, from the Metropolitan Area to the Four Seas, there is no place without a school, which is none other than the ancient institution of district schools (dangxiang and suixu). In the examination categories of those earlier times, candidates were selected for their literary embellishments and parallel phrasing, to the point where men of outstanding talent blushed with shame and disdained to participate; today, however, since the schools instruct people in classical learning, the examination categories likewise select scholars on the basis of classical learning. Scholars do not practice any writings other than those of the Odes, Documents, Rites, and Music, nor do they discuss anything other than the Way of Yao, Shun, …

title: 天順六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
周孔之道不談脩之於家者而可用
之於
國即古賓興賢能攷其德行道藝之意
矣肆惟
皇上又慮學政久而怠弛也日者復設憲
臣重加委任務在督興賢才俾底成
效
仁君之心無所不用其極如此以故賢才
===
之出彬彬濟濟有卷阿棫樸所詠之
盛選者如陟崑崙遊鄧林萬金之璧
千尋之名材隨所取而有焉於是豈
不足以驗
天眷之厚乎向若
天眷我
國家徒與之以祥瑞雖麒麟鳳凰甘露
靈芝駢臻迭降何補於治惟賢才之
alt_text:
周孔之道不談脩之於家者而可用
之於
國卽古賓興賢能攷其德行道藝之意
矣肆惟
皇上又慮學政久而怠弛也日者復設憲
臣重加委任務在督興賢才俾底成
效
===
仁君之心無所不用其極如此以故賢才
之出彬彬濟濟有卷阿棫樸所詠之
盛選者如陟崑崙遊鄧林薦金之璧
千尋之名材隨所取而有焉於是豈
不足以驗
天眷之厚乎向若
天眷我
國家徒與之以祥瑞雖麒麟鳳凰甘露
靈芝駢臻迭降何補於治惟賢才之
punctuated: 周孔之道不談，脩之於家者，而可用之於國，即古賓興賢能，攷其德行道藝之意矣。肆惟皇上又慮學政久而怠弛也，日者復設憲臣，重加委任，務在督興賢才，俾底成效。仁君之心，無所不用其極如此，以故賢才之出，彬彬濟濟，有《卷阿》、《棫樸》所詠之盛。選者如陟崑崙、遊鄧林，萬金之璧、千尋之名材，隨所取而有焉。於是豈不足以驗天眷之厚乎？向若天眷我國家，徒與之以祥瑞，雖麒麟、鳳凰、甘露、靈芝駢臻迭降，何補於治？惟賢才之
translation_en: …the Way of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, they do not discuss; what they cultivate at home can be put to use in the state. This is precisely the ancient principle of presenting the worthy and able as guests and examining their moral conduct, mastery of the Way, and practical arts. Now, His Majesty the Emperor, concerned lest the administration of schools grow lax over time, recently appointed censorial officials and entrusted them with weighty responsibilities, charging them with supervising and encouraging worthy talents so as to bring about tangible results. The mind of our benevolent ruler spares no effort in going to the utmost like this. For this reason, worthy talents have emerged in refined and abundant numbers, matching the flourishing state celebrated in the odes "Juan'e" (Curving Slope) and "Yupu" (Thickly Growing Oaks). Those who select them are like travelers ascending the Kunlun Mountains or roaming the Deng Forest: jade disks worth ten thousand pieces of gold and prized timber a thousand fathoms tall are there to be had wherever one reaches for them. Is this not sufficient to verify the depth of Heaven's favor? Suppose Heaven, in favoring our dynasty, merely bestowed auspicious portents upon it: even if unicorns (qilin), phoenixes, sweet dew, and numinous mushrooms arrived side by side and descended in turn, of what help would they be to governance? Only when worthy talents…

title: 天順六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
盛則可以基億萬年之太平無疑矣
雖然均是人也而以賢才稱豈徒負
美名以動人觀聽哉必其德與能有
以過乎人也今諸士子發身科目固
皆勉於德而脩其能矣行將入官效
用有日思
君上作養之恩體
天眷之厚盍亦知所以圖報乎圖報何如
===
古之君子有耻其君不為堯舜者一
夫不獲則曰時予之辜其意豈慕乎
爵祿之崇功名之顯以為不如是不
足以盡吾為臣之心爾噫士而知此
則凡所以夙夜匪懈以事其
君者自不容於不勉矣語云有君如此其
忍負之詩曰不愧于人不畏于天敢
預以為諸士子誦亦竊願與有官者
alt_text:
盛則可以基億萬年之太平無疑矣
雖然均是人也而以賢才稱豈徒負
美名以動人觀聽哉必其德與能有
以過乎人也今諸士子發身科目固
皆勉於德而備其能矣行將入官效
用有日思
君上作養之恩體
天眷之厚盍亦知所以圖報乎圖報何如
===
古之君子有恥其君不爲堯舜者一
夫不獲則曰時予之辜其意豈慕乎
爵祿之崇功名之顯以爲不如是不
足以盡吾爲臣之心爾噫士而知此
則凡所以夙夜匪懈以事其
君者自不容於不勉矣語云有君如此其
忍負之詩曰不愧于人不畏于天敢
預以爲諸士子誦亦竊願與有官者
punctuated: 盛，則可以基億萬年之太平，無疑矣。雖然，均是人也，而以賢才稱，豈徒負美名以動人觀聽哉？必其德與能有以過乎人也。今諸士子發身科目，固皆勉於德而脩其能矣。行將入官，效用有日，思君上作養之恩，體天眷之厚，盍亦知所以圖報乎？圖報何如？古之君子，有耻其君不為堯、舜者，一夫不獲，則曰：「時予之辜。」其意豈慕乎爵祿之崇、功名之顯？以為不如是，不足以盡吾為臣之心爾。噫！士而知此，則凡所以夙夜匪懈以事其君者，自不容於不勉矣。語云：「有君如此，其忍負之？」《詩》曰：「不愧于人，不畏于天。」敢預以為諸士子誦，亦竊願與有官者
translation_en: … abundance of worthy talents can without a doubt lay the foundation for ten thousand myriad years of great peace. Even so, all are human beings alike; when some are spoken of as worthy talents, is it merely that they bear a fine reputation to stir people's eyes and ears? Surely it is because their virtue and ability surpass those of others. Now, as these gentlemen launch their careers through the examination system, they have certainly all striven in virtue and cultivated their abilities. Soon they will enter officialdom, and the day when they render service is at hand. Reflecting upon the Sovereign's grace in nurturing them and appreciating the depth of Heaven's favor, why should they not also know how to plan their repayment? And how should one plan to repay it? Among the noble men of antiquity, there were those who were ashamed if their ruler did not become a Yao or a Shun, and if a single common man failed to find his place, they would say, "It is my fault." Was their intent to covet lofty rank and emolument, or the splendor of merit and fame? They simply held that anything less would be insufficient to fulfill their hearts as subjects. Alas! If a scholar understands this, then in all whereby he serves his Sovereign without slackening from dawn to night, he naturally cannot fail to exert himself. As the saying goes, "Having a ruler such as this, how could one bear to fail him?" And the Book of Odes (Shijing) says, "Not ashamed before men, not fearful before Heaven." I venture to recite these words in advance for the gentlemen, and I also privately wish that together with those who hold office…

title: 天順六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
子之燕居申申如也夭夭如也
天地之道可一言而盡也其為物不貳則
其生物不測天地之道博也厚也高也
明也悠也久也今夫天斯昭昭之多及
其無窮也日月星辰繫焉萬物覆焉今
夫地一撮土之多及其廣厚載華嶽而
===
不重振河海而不洩萬物載焉
聖人既竭目力焉繼之以規矩準繩以為
方員平直不可勝用也既竭耳力焉繼
之以六律正五音不可勝用也既竭心
思焉繼之以不忍人之政而仁覆天下
矣故曰為高必因丘陵為下必因川澤
為政不因先王之道可謂智乎
易

第壹場
四書
子之燕居申申如也夭夭如也
天地之道可一言而盡也其爲物不貳則
其生物不測天地之道博也厚也高也
明也悠也久也今夫天斯昭昭之多及
其無窮也日月星辰繫焉萬物覆焉今
夫地一撮土之多及其廣厚載華嶽而
不重振河海而不洩萬物載焉
===
聖人既竭目力焉繼之以規矩準繩以爲
方員平直不可勝用也既竭耳力焉繼
之以六律正五音不可勝用也既竭心
思焉繼之以不忍人之政而仁覆天下
矣故曰爲高必因丘陵爲下必因川澤
爲政不因先王之道可謂智乎
易
punctuated:
第壹塲

四書

子之燕居，申申如也，夭夭如也。

天地之道，可一言而盡也。其為物不貳，則其生物不測。天地之道，博也，厚也，高也，明也，悠也，久也。今夫天，斯昭昭之多，及其無窮也，日月星辰繫焉，萬物覆焉。今夫地，一撮土之多，及其廣厚，載華嶽而不重，振河海而不洩，萬物載焉。

聖人既竭目力焉，繼之以規矩準繩，以為方員平直，不可勝用也；既竭耳力焉，繼之以六律，正五音，不可勝用也；既竭心思焉，繼之以不忍人之政，而仁覆天下矣。故曰，為高必因丘陵，為下必因川澤。為政不因先王之道，可謂智乎？

易
translation_en:
First Session

The Four Books

"When the Master was unoccupied with business, his manner was easy, and he looked pleased." (Analects 7.4)

"The Way of Heaven and Earth may be completely declared in one sentence. They are without any doubleness, and so they produce things in a manner that is unfathomable. The Way of Heaven and Earth is large and substantial, high and brilliant, far-reaching and long-enduring. The sky now before us is only this bright shining spot; but when viewed in its inexhaustible extent, the sun, moon, stars, and constellations of the zodiac are suspended in it, and all things are overspread by it. The earth before us is but a handful of soil; but when viewed in all its breadth and thickness, it sustains Mount Hua and the other sacred peaks without feeling their weight, contains the rivers and seas without their leaking away, and sustains all things." (Doctrine of the Mean 26)

"When the sages had used the vigor of their eyes, they called in to their aid the compass, the square, the level, and the line, to make things square, round, level, and straight: the use of the instruments is inexhaustible. When they had used their power of hearing to the utmost, they called in the six pitch-pipes to determine the five notes: the use of them is inexhaustible. When they had exerted to the utmost the thoughts of their hearts, they called in to their aid a government that could not endure to witness the sufferings of men, and their benevolence overspread the world. Hence we have the saying: 'To raise a thing high, we must begin from the top of a mound or a hill; to dig to a great depth, we must commence in the low ground of a stream or a marsh.' Can he be pronounced wise who, in the exercise of government, does not proceed according to the Way of the former kings?" (Mencius 4A.1)

Classic of Changes (Yi)

嘉會足以合禮，利物足以和義。
當位貞吉，以正邦也。
在天成象，在地成形，變化見矣。是故剛柔相摩，八卦相盪，鼓之以雷霆，潤之以風雨，日月運行，一寒一暑，乾道成男，坤道成女。
艮以止之，兌以說之，乾以君之，坤以藏之。

書

侯以明之。
終始慎厥與，惟明明后。先王惟時懋敬厥德，克配上帝。今王嗣有令緒，尚監茲哉。若升高，必自下；若陟遐，必自邇。
汝劼毖殷獻臣，侯、甸、男、衛；矧太史友、內史友，越獻臣百宗工；矧惟爾事，服休服采；矧惟若疇：圻父薄違，農父若保，宏父定辟；矧汝剛制于酒。
translation_en:
"An excellence of assemblage is sufficient to accord with ritual propriety; benefiting all things is sufficient to harmonize with righteousness."
"Being in the proper position, firm correctness brings good fortune: thereby one rectifies the state."
"In heaven, images are formed; on earth, shapes are formed; and thus changes and transformations are made manifest. Therefore, the firm and the yielding rub against each other, and the eight trigrams agitate one another. Things are roused by thunder and lightning, moistened by wind and rain; the sun and moon move in their courses, producing now cold, now heat; the way of Qian constitutes the male, and the way of Kun constitutes the female."
"Gen serves to bring them to a standstill; Dui serves to give them pleasure; Qian serves to rule over them; Kun serves to store them up."

Book of Documents (Shu)

"The target for archery serves to make evident their virtue."
"To be cautious from beginning to end about whom one associates with—such is the truly enlightened sovereign. The former kings devoted themselves at all times to reverently cultivating their virtue, and so were able to be worthy counterparts to the Lord on High. Now the king has succeeded to this fine inheritance; may he take this as his mirror! It is like ascending to a height: one must begin from below; it is like traveling to a distant place: one must begin from what is near."
"Do you firmly caution the worthy ministers of Yin, and the lords of the hou, dian, nan, and wei domains; how much more so your friends the Grand Scribe (taishi) and the Scribe of the Interior (neishi), along with your worthy ministers and the hundred respected artisans; how much more so your personal attendants, who serve you in leisure and in active affairs; how much more so your peers the senior ministers: the Minister of War (qifu), who checks transgressions; the Minister of Agriculture (nongfu), who conforms to and protects the people; and the Minister of Works (hongfu), who establishes the laws; and how much more should you yourself resolutely restrain yourself from wine!"

Question: Since antiquity, those who have excelled at governing the world have always guided the people by relying on the foundation of popular virtue, and thus achieved true kingship without toil. This is just what Confucius meant when he said, "The teachings of the former kings were accomplished without severity, and their governance brought order without harshness, because what they relied upon was the root." If so, the foundation of the people's virtue surely lies in nothing other than filial piety; yet whereby can the reality of the former kings' accomplished teachings and well-ordered governance actually be seen? Humbly reflecting on our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu, the Hongwu Emperor), when he founded the dynasty and bequeathed its legitimacy, out of concern that his officials and people had not yet fulfilled filial piety to the utmost, he composed the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao) and displayed the chapter elucidating filial piety to the entire realm. translation_en: …the Lu calendar's placement of intercalary months was improper—on what basis was this actually said? Confucius once stated, "I have obtained the seasonal calendar of Xia," and he also composed the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), using the sun and moon to fix the calendrical calculations. Yet scholars of later ages claimed that the calendrical methods of the Three Dynasties were not transmitted, and that the disciples of Confucius never spoke of them; is this view right or wrong? From the Qin dynasty onward, calendars were never more complete than under the Han and the Tang. The Han calendar underwent four changes in all, with the Grand Inception (Taichu) calendar being the finest; the Tang calendar underwent eight changes in all, with the Great Expansion (Dayan) calendar being the finest. Since the two differ, may their details also be heard? When Sima Qian 司馬遷 wrote the Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), there was a "Treatise on Pitch-Pipes" (Lüshu) and a "Treatise on the Calendar" (Lishu), taking the pitch-pipes as the root of the myriad affairs, upon which calendrical methods are founded. Therefore, the treatises in the histories of the Former and Later Han, Jin, and Sui all combined pitch-pipes and the calendar, whereas the New History of the Tang (Xin Tangshu) alone had a treatise on the calendar without a treatise on pitch-pipes—why is that? Now, the calendar involves the solar trajectory (richan), lunar path (yueli), solar excess (qiying), lunar deficiency (shuoxu), the day divisor (rifa), the Dipper fraction (doufen), the intercalary remainder (runyu), and the precession of the equinoxes (suicha), all of which are matters that Confucian scholars ought to investigate. In later ages, there were those above who reformed the calendar, yet they delighted in sycophancy and loved flattery, not originally establishing it to "respectfully grant the seasons"; and there were those below who devised calendars, yet they coveted favor and craved profit, not originally measuring the rightness or wrongness of their methods—these are certainly unworthy of esteem. From the Song to the Yuan, among Confucian scholars who were well-versed in calendrical methods and became renowned in the historical records,…

…who were they? At present, the Sage is on the throne, ordering the seven regulators [the sun, moon, and five planets] and fixing the four seasons; in all matters of revering Heaven and laboring for the people, there is nothing to which he does not devote his mind, and toward this he is especially earnest. Question: In antiquity, the Way and its Virtue were unified so as to make customs uniform. When scholars lived in those times, the places where they were quartered were not different, the methods by which they were nurtured were not different, and the paths by which they were selected were not different. Consequently, people had settled aims and customs had no divergent preferences; indeed, they did not even know the name "heterodoxy," how much less was there any so-called "teaching of heterodoxy"! After the Way and its arts split apart, heterodoxies arose side by side. This is what Han Changli [Han Yu 韓愈] meant by saying, "In antiquity the teaching was one; today the teachings are three." When teachings reach three in number, the disunity of the Way and its Virtue is extreme indeed—how then can customs be made uniform? Even so, how is this true only of heterodoxies? … the learning of the Confucian scholar.” The learning of the Confucian scholar possesses both substance and practical function; in its preservation there is a root, and in its practice there is an order. Heterodox doctrines are not so. Yet where they are not so, they must have some specious resemblance to the truth—can this be pointed out and discussed? Now, the ways and arts of the world have already been split into three, and the learning of us Confucians is moreover unable to synthesize and return to unity. As for those heterodoxies, there is indeed nothing to be done about them; as for ourselves, if we definitely wish to unite the ancestral lineage and gather the primal source so as to return to unity, not sinking into the flowery extravagance of branches and leaves or the coarse vulgarity of rote learning between mouth and ear, causing our Way to be illuminated, perversity and evil to cease of themselves, and customs to become uniform of themselves—there must be a way to achieve this. You gentlemen are students of Confucian learning, and therefore I venture to put this question to you.

Question: Scholars study antiquity in order to enter officialdom, so contemporary affairs cannot go unknown to them. May we tentatively deliberate upon the essentials? Performance evaluation is the means to investigate the governance of officials. Yet among today’s authorities, who knows how many are worthy or unworthy, while blame and praise mostly arise from likes and dislikes driven by personal favoritism, and merits and faults are uniformly judged by a single day’s discussion. By what means can we ensure that those who toil in heart to nurture the people are not overlooked in inquiries and inspections, and that those who pander to win reputation cannot advance by undeserved luck? Schools are the means to nurture worthy talents. Yet today…

title: 天順六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
太學生徒無慮數千而精銳罷於歲月
之拘歷才智迫於資用之不給何以使
長安困厄之賢皆有所激勵唱義仁勇
之士不至於淹滯歟
國家設立都司分遣邊將欲其保障一方也
今遇一方小警輒勤
王師遠征而西北用兵糜費尤甚何以使幹
不庭方者悉能有備圖上邊奏者能省
===
費而息患歟漕運取粟於民輸輓以兵
欲其兵民兼濟也今值兌粟之際民既
出其廩餼餘而輸納之時兵多窘於稱貸
何以使沾體塗足者不至重困汎舟勞
役者不至疲憊歟至於刑罰以謹民命
朝廷毎断一獄必詳審而後行然窮鄉小民
情弗上達者多矣何以使白日受誣者
皆有所控訴科派以資

punctuated: 太學生徒無慮數千，而精銳罷於歲月之拘歷，才智迫於資用之不給，何以使長安困厄之賢皆有所激勵，唱義仁勇之士不至於淹滯歟？國家設立都司，分遣邊將，欲其保障一方也。今遇一方小警，輒勤王師遠征，而西北用兵糜費尤甚，何以使幹不庭方者悉能有備，圖上邊奏者能省費而息患歟？漕運取粟於民，輸輓以兵，欲其兵民兼濟也。今值兌粟之際，民既出其廩餼餘，而輸納之時，兵多窘於稱貸，何以使沾體塗足者不至重困，汎舟勞役者不至疲憊歟？至於刑罰以謹民命，朝廷毎断一獄，必詳審而後行；然窮鄉小民，情弗上達者多矣，何以使白日受誣者皆有所控訴？科派以資
translation_en: … students in the Directorate of Education number roughly several thousand, yet their finest energies are worn down by the constraints of years spent serving internships, and their talents and intelligence are pressed by inadequate stipends and provisions. How can we ensure that worthy men suffering hardship in the capital are all roused to encouragement, and that gentlemen who champion righteousness, benevolence, and courage do not languish without advancement? The state established Regional Military Commissions and dispatched frontier generals to various posts, intending that they safeguard their respective regions. Nowadays, whenever a minor alarm arises in any region, the imperial armies are immediately troubled with distant expeditions, and the wasteful expenditure of military operations in the northwest is especially severe. How can we ensure that those charged with rectifying unsubmissive quarters are all fully prepared, and that those who submit strategic memorials on frontier affairs are able to curtail expenses and put an end to calamities? Grain transport collects grain from the common people and transports it by means of soldiers, intending that soldiers and civilians mutually benefit. Nowadays, at the time of the grain transfer, the people already pay an extra surtax for rations and wastage, while at the time of delivery to the granaries, the soldiers are mostly driven into distress by borrowing at interest. How can we ensure that those who drench their bodies and mire their feet in the fields are not doubly burdened, and that those who toil in navigating the transport boats do not fall into exhaustion? As for punishments and penalties, which are meant to treat the lives of the people with utmost care: whenever the court decides a criminal case, it invariably conducts a thorough review before carrying it out; yet among the common folk in remote villages, there are many whose grievances fail to reach those above. How can we ensure that those who suffer false accusations in broad daylight all have an avenue of appeal? Requisitions and levies are meant to supply …

title: 天順六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
國用
朝廷所需不能什一然有司因而掊尅者夥
矣何以使登壟罔利者不肆其侵暴歟
茲數者皆時務之所當講者諸生能有
以處之則他日從政可迎刄而解矣幸
直言之毋隱
問
國家財賦所入者衆矣而浙右之田租淮南
===
之鹽課幾當天下之半斯皆在今畿甸
間乃古揚州之域也考之禹貢揚州之
田下下而比他州為最劣周禮職方氏
所載其地宜稻而他種皆非所有夫田
居九等之末而僅有五穀之一其地力
薄矣乃今蘇松常鎮四郡封域之限較
之他郡不加廣而歲輸數百萬石總天
下之田租殆居十四五焉民力無乃困

===

間乃古揚州之域也考之禹貢揚州之
田下下而比他州為最劣周禮職方氏
所載其地宜稻而他種皆非所有夫田
居九等之末而僅有五穀之一其地力

之他郡不加廣而歲輸數百萬石總天
下之田租殆居十四五焉民力無乃困
punctuated:
國用，朝廷所需不能什一，然有司因而掊尅者夥矣。何以使登壟罔利者不肆其侵暴歟？茲數者，皆時務之所當講者。諸生能有以處之，則他日從政，可迎刄而解矣。幸直言之，毋隱。

問：國家財賦所入者衆矣，而浙右之田租、淮南之鹽課，幾當天下之半。斯皆在今畿甸間，乃古揚州之域也。考之《禹貢》，揚州之田下下，而比他州為最劣；《周禮》職方氏所載，其地宜稻，而他種皆非所有。夫田居九等之末，而僅有五穀之一，其地力薄矣。乃今蘇、松、常、鎮四郡，封域之限較之他郡不加廣，而歲輸數百萬石，總天下之田租，殆居十四五焉。民力無乃困
translation_en:
… state expenditures, what the Court actually requires is not even one-tenth, yet the local authorities take the opportunity to extort a great deal more. How can we ensure that those who monopolize the market to net profits do not freely engage in such predatory abuses? These several matters are all current affairs that ought to be discussed. If you students have ways to deal with them, then in the future when you engage in governance, you will be able to resolve problems as easily as a blade splitting bamboo. Please speak forthrightly and conceal nothing.

Question: The sources of the state's financial revenues are numerous, yet the land tax of Zheyou [western Zhejiang and southern Jiangsu] and the salt tax of Huainan nearly equal half of the entire empire's total. Both of these lie within the present Capital Metropolitan Area (Jidian), which was the territory of ancient Yangzhou. Examining the Tribute of Yu (Yugong), the fields of Yangzhou were graded "lower-lowest" (xiaxia), making them the most inferior compared to other provinces; according to what is recorded under the Director of Regions (Zhifang shi) in the Rites of Zhou (Zhouli), the land is suitable for rice, while lacking all other crops. Now, with its fields ranked at the very bottom of the nine grades and producing only one of the five grains, the productivity of its soil was meager indeed. Yet today, in the four prefectures of Suzhou, Songjiang, Changzhou, and Zhenjiang, the extent of their territorial boundaries is no broader than that of other prefectures, while their annual tax grain deliveries amount to several million piculs (shi)—accounting for nearly four- or five-tenths of the total land tax of the entire empire. Is the strength of the people not exhausted…

title: 天順六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
歟不幸而水旱頻仍粒米匱乏不知何
以裕
國用而安民生也管子海王之篇煮海止於
齊地漢之鹽官在會稽者唯海鹽有之
皆非今淮地也夫土地生殖古今所同
古既無有今亦宜然矣乃今維揚淮安
兩郡濱海之民比之他郡不加多而歲
課數十萬引舉天下之鹽利殆居十五
===
六焉民力無乃竭歟不幸而雨水不常
亭戶流徙不知何以通商旅而給民食
也雖然事之所起必有所因弊之所生
必有其故聞之不若見之之切言之非
若行之之艱諸士子或生長於斯或密
邇其地積學待問天下之事展轉於其
心也久矣況其切近者乎將必有善處
之術

===

亭户流徙不知何以通商旅而給民食
也雖然事之所起必有所因弊之所生

之術
punctuated: 歟？不幸而水旱頻仍，粒米匱乏，不知何以裕國用而安民生也？《管子》〈海王〉之篇，煮海止於齊地；漢之鹽官在會稽者，唯海鹽有之，皆非今淮地也。夫土地生殖，古今所同；古既無有，今亦宜然矣。乃今維揚、淮安兩郡濱海之民，比之他郡不加多，而歲課數十萬引，舉天下之鹽利殆居十五六焉。民力無乃竭歟？不幸而雨水不常，亭戶流徙，不知何以通商旅而給民食也？雖然，事之所起必有所因，弊之所生必有其故。聞之不若見之之切，言之非若行之之艱。諸士子或生長於斯，或密邇其地，積學待問，天下之事展轉於其心也久矣，況其切近者乎？將必有善處之術。
translation_en: … [Must not the people's strength be] distressed? If, unfortunately, floods and droughts occur repeatedly and grain becomes scarce, I do not know how we are to enrich state finances and bring peace to the people's livelihood? In the "Sea King" (Haiwang) chapter of the Guanzi, boiling seawater for salt was limited to the territory of Qi; during the Han dynasty, the Salt Officials (yanguan) in Kuaiji existed only at Haiyan—none of these were in the present Huai region. Now, the productive capacity of the land is the same in ancient and modern times; since it did not exist in antiquity, it ought to be so today as well. Yet today the coastal populace of the two prefectures of Weiyang (Yangzhou) and Huai'an is no more numerous than that of other prefectures, while their annual quota reaches several hundred thousand yin (salt certificates), accounting for nearly fifty or sixty percent of the salt revenues of the entire realm. Must not the people's strength be exhausted? If, unfortunately, rainfall is irregular and the saltern households (tinghu) flee and scatter, I do not know how we are to keep merchant traffic flowing and supply the people with salt for their food? Even so, where affairs arise there must be a cause, and where abuses emerge there must be a reason. Hearing of them is not as immediate as seeing them; speaking of them is not as difficult as putting them into practice. You gentlemen were either born and raised here or live in close proximity to these places. Having accumulated learning while awaiting inquiry, the affairs of the realm have been turned over in your minds for a long time—how much more so those matters that are right before you? You will surely have sound methods for dealing with them.

title: 天順六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
四書義
子之燕居申申如也夭夭如也
任彦常
同考試官教諭蕭批此題作者不失之泛則失之畧惟此篇詞意
春容筆力高古以中和貫之誠有學之士
同考試官教諭王批此題似平易寔難措辭作者必須偶得
此篇詞既暢達又講歸盛德之至夫何忝
考試官檢討邢批能形容聖人燕居氣象得當時門人之意矣
考試官脩撰劉批視他作騁浮語者不同
===
觀聖人在閒暇之時其容色一中和之著夫聖人之
德盛於內則雖閒居之時自有中和之氣著於外也
門人特記以示人詎無意乎思昔弟子形容聖人有
言其盛德光輝接於人者矣有記其容色言動著於
事者焉今而曰子之燕居申申夭夭何也蓋燕居乃
閒暇無事之時非接人待物之際斯時也常人不失
之怠肆必入於嚴厲欲其容色一適於中和不可得
已惟聖人盛德之至随寓而安不怠肆也而亦不嚴
厲其容之見於身者則動靜舒徐而迫遽之不形四

四書義

任彦常

Observing the sage in his moments of leisure, his demeanor and countenance were entirely a manifestation of equilibrium and harmony. Now, since the sage's virtue was abundant within, even when dwelling at leisure, thevital force of equilibrium and harmony naturally manifested without. When his disciples specially recorded this to show to others, how could it have been without purpose? When we reflect on how the disciples of old described the sage, there were instances where they spoke of the splendor of his abundant virtue in his dealings with others, and instances where they recorded his demeanor, countenance, speech, and actions as manifested in affairs. Why, then, is it here said: "When the Master was unoccupied with business, he was easy and looked pleased"? For dwelling unoccupied is a time of leisure without affairs, not an occasion of dealing with people or attending to things. At such a time, ordinary people, if they do not err by falling into laxity and indulgence, inevitably slip into sternness and severity; should one wish their demeanor and countenance to accord entirely with equilibrium and harmony, it cannot be attained. Only the sage, at the utmost perfection of abundant virtue, is at peace wherever he finds himself—neither lax and indulgent, nor stern and severe. … limbs were relaxed and unhurried, with nothing cramped or constrained. This was not a deliberate effort to appear relaxed, but simply the natural manifestation of the vital energy of equilibrium and harmony. As for his countenance as it appeared upon his face, it was effortlessly joyful and pleased, no less than the mildness of a spring breeze; it was affable and cheerfully content, just like the warmth of the morning sun. This was not a deliberate effort to appear joyful, but likewise the natural expression of the vital energy of equilibrium and harmony.

His disciples observed this, yet found it difficult to put into words. Thus they did not merely say "relaxed" (shenshen), but also said "cheerful" (yaoyao), because the meaning of "relaxed" did not fully exhaust it, and so they further added the words "cheerful." And they did not merely say "relaxed" and "cheerful," but added "like" (ru) to the first and "like" (ru) to the second, because the subtlety of such naturalness was even more beyond what words could describe. Alas! May they not be called keen observers of the Sage who applied their minds with subtlety and care?

Even so, people merely know that when the Sage was at leisure, his bearing was relaxed and his countenance joyful, without knowing that this arose from the manifestation of his equilibrium and harmony; and people merely know of the manifestation of the Sage's equilibrium and harmony, without knowing that it was rooted in the perfection of his abundant virtue. If we examine other chapters [of the Analects], one says: "The Master is warm yet厳 (strict/dignified), awe-inspiring yet not fierce, respectful yet at ease." Another says: "Looked at from a distance, he is imposing; approached closely, he is warm; when one listens to his words, they are exacting." All of these are simply the natural tallies of abundant virtue. Those who set their will upon learning ought to immerse their minds in this.

Creation is unified in sincerity, and its efficacy and operation are unfathomable; therefore Heaven and Earth are each able to reach the utmost of their flourishing and manifest the work of generating things. It is fitting indeed that Zisi spoke thus to illuminate the efficacy and operation of utmost sincerity without cease. Moreover, that which stands firm and is positioned above is Heaven; although the Way of Heaven is great, what allows it to be summed up in a single word goes no further than sincerity. That which lies compliant and is positioned below is Earth; although the Way of Earth is great, what allows it to be summed up in a single word likewise goes no further than sincerity. Far-reaching to the utmost of its reach, enduring to the utmost of its endurance—is this not that by which heaven and earth are heaven and earth? Now, the Way of heaven and earth each reaches the utmost of its flourishing like this. Therefore, if one points to a single spot of heaven and speaks of it, one sees nothing more than a gleaming little light; yet when one takes its entirety and observes it, then all the revolutions of the sun and moon and the array of the stars and constellations are suspended above, and there is nothing among the myriad things that it does not overspread. If one points to a single spot of earth and speaks of it, one sees nothing more than a mere handful of soil; yet when one takes its entirety and observes it, it supports Mount Hua without finding it heavy, contains the rivers and seas without letting them leak away, and there is nothing among the myriad things that it does not sustain. Such is the wondrous achievement of heaven and earth in generating things. Were it not for utmost sincerity without cease, how could this be brought about? Examining the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong), this chapter speaks of the Way of Heaven. Shi Huai 石淮

Associate Examiner Instructor Zhou 周 comments: Topics from the Mencius have many threads and are the hardest to pull together. This essay is thorough and clear in its exposition, with a continuous flow of thought and style that sets it apart from the other compositions; it ought to be selected for publication.
Examiner Examining Editor Xing 邢 comments: Its conception is lofty and its diction antique, far surpassing the other compositions.
Examiner Senior Compiler Liu 劉 comments: It succeeds in elucidating the sages' intent in establishing laws and why later generations ought to model themselves on antiquity; it truly deserves to be selected.

Having explained in detail that the sages had a basis for establishing laws whose reach is inexhaustible, the Great Worthy [Mencius] necessarily cites evidence to state that if a ruler governs without following antiquity, his mind is unwise. Now, why did the sages, having already exhausted their own strength, go on to create laws and standards? It was solely because they wished their benefit to extend to all under heaven and to later generations. If those who engage in governance in later times do not follow and employ them, how then can they be considered wise? In wishing to exhort men, the Great Worthy necessarily quoted an ancient saying to substantiate his words; his meaning was profound indeed.

Of old, Mencius's meaning was as if to say: When the sages of antiquity looked afar with clear sight, nothing square, round, level, or straight could escape them—they had indeed exhausted the strength of their eyes. Yet, still considering this insufficient to reach all under heaven and extend to later generations, they devised the compass, square, level, and marking-line to continue their work; thus all under heaven who wished to make things square, round, level, or straight unfailingly took them as their model, and their utility became inexhaustible. When they listened with acute hearing, no subtle essence of the five notes went unexamined—they had indeed exhausted the strength of their ears. Yet, still considering this insufficient to reach all under heaven and extend to later generations, they devised the six pitch-pipes to continue their work; thus all under heaven who wished to rectify the five notes unfailingly took them as their standard, and their utility became boundless. As for cherishing and protecting the common people and showing kindness to widows and widowers, they had likewise exhausted the strength of their minds and thoughts; …

title: 天順六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
然猶以為天下之大後世之遠吾心之仁不能遍及
也故又制為不忍人之政以繼之如井田學校之類
則政之所存即仁之所寓天下雖大而聖澤霑被為
有餘後世雖遠而仁恩所及為無間矣是則聖人立
法之意如此後之為政者顧可不因而用之乎於是
復引古語而言彼為高者必因夫丘陵何也以丘陵
本高因之則用力少而成功多也彼為下者必因夫
川澤何也以川澤本下因之則用力省而獲效廣也
先王之道即聖人所立之仁政也規矩準繩六律皆
===
仁政之不可闕者苟徇己私而不因則無以制器審
音是為高者之不如謂之明理不可也井田學校尤
仁政之所先務者苟執己見而不遵則無以教養天
下是為下者之不若謂之有識又可乎哉孟子言此
欲人以仁心仁聞行先王之政至矣大抵此章之旨
以仁心仁政不可偏廢故前既言徒善不足以為政
徒法不能以自行至此又本先王立法之意以勉人
噫使當時之君有能行其言者則戰國可轉為三代
之盛惜乎其不能用也

punctuated: 然猶以為天下之大、後世之遠，吾心之仁不能遍及也，故又制為不忍人之政以繼之，如井田、學校之類。則政之所存，即仁之所寓，天下雖大而聖澤霑被為有餘，後世雖遠而仁恩所及為無間矣。是則聖人立法之意如此，後之為政者，顧可不因而用之乎？於是復引古語而言：彼為高者，必因夫丘陵，何也？以丘陵本高，因之則用力少而成功多也；彼為下者，必因夫川澤，何也？以川澤本下，因之則用力省而獲效廣也。先王之道，即聖人所立之仁政也。規矩、準繩、六律，皆仁政之不可闕者，苟徇己私而不因，則無以制器審音，是為高者之不如，謂之明理，不可也；井田、學校，尤仁政之所先務者，苟執己見而不遵，則無以教養天下，是為下者之不若，謂之有識，又可乎哉？孟子言此，欲人以仁心、仁聞行先王之政，至矣。大抵此章之旨，以仁心、仁政不可偏廢，故前既言「徒善不足以為政，徒法不能以自行」，至此又本先王立法之意以勉人。噫！使當時之君有能行其言者，則戰國可轉為三代之盛，惜乎其不能用也。
translation_en:
Yet because the world is so vast and posterity so distant, they still felt that the benevolence of their own hearts could not reach everywhere. Therefore, they further instituted governance that cannot bear to see the suffering of others to continue it, such as the well-field system and schools. Thus, wherever such governance exists, there benevolence resides; though the world be vast, the moisturizing grace of the sages is more than sufficient to cover it, and though posterity be distant, the reach of their benevolent favor is uninterrupted. Such, then, was the intention of the sages in establishing laws; how could later rulers fail to build upon and employ them?

Thereupon, he again cites an ancient saying, stating: Why must those who raise up mounds make use of hills and knolls? Because hills and knolls are naturally high, and by building upon them, one expends little effort yet achieves much. Why must those who excavate lowlands make use of streams and marshes? Because streams and marshes are naturally low, and by building upon them, one spares effort yet reaps broad results. The Way of the former kings is none other than the benevolent governance established by the sages. The compass, square, level, marking-line, and the six pitch-pipes are all indispensable to benevolent governance; if one indulges personal selfishness and does not rely upon them, there will be no means to fashion implements or determine musical pitches—being inferior even to one who raises up mounds, how could one be called discerning of principle? The well-field system and schools are especially the foremost priorities of benevolent governance; if one clings to personal opinions and does not follow them, there will be no means to educate and nourish the world—failing even to match one who excavates lowlands, how could one be called perceptive? In saying this, Mencius wished for rulers to carry out the governance of the former kings through a benevolent heart and a reputation for benevolence; his intention was utmost.

In general, the main purport of this chapter is that a benevolent heart and benevolent governance cannot be one-sidedly neglected. Hence, having earlier stated that "goodness alone is not sufficient for the exercise of government; laws alone cannot carry themselves into practice," when he reaches this point he again grounds his argument in the intention of the former kings in establishing laws so as to encourage people. Alas! Had the rulers of that time been able to put his words into practice, the Warring States period could have been transformed into the flourishing prosperity of the Three Dynasties. What a pity that they were unable to employ them!

「嘉會足以合禮，利物足以和義。」

惟有以周於用，斯足以會夫理。蓋嘉會、利物，用之見於事者也；禮、義，理之具於心者也。體乾之君子，既有以周於用，則豈不足以會夫理乎？《文言》聖人釋乾之「亨」、「利」，而推之人事者如此。蓋嘗觀之，禮者，人心所具之理也。君子之為禮，果何如邪？俾凡綱常倫理皆有以盡其道，動容周旋皆有以中乎節，舉天下之事無一而不致其美焉，是則所謂「嘉會」矣。君子之嘉會如此，故身之所履者皆天理之節文，心之所安者亦人

Exposition on the Book of Changes (Yijing)

"Excellence of assembly is sufficient to conform to ritual propriety; benefitting things is sufficient to harmonize with righteousness."

By Yu Bi 於弼

Comment by Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor (xundao) Pan 潘: [On this topic, people can generally explain the section on "benefitting things," but they mostly fail to grasp the true meaning of the words "excellence of assembly" (jiahui). This essay explains and connects them clearly, and furthermore takes the former Confucian scholars' doctrine of "proceeding from function to principle" as the lifeblood running through the entire piece; compared to this, those trivial attempts are not worth discussing.]
Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor (jiaoyu) Wu 吳: [This topic has a pivotal point which writers carelessly fail to examine, thus mostly missing the main idea. Clear in principle and lucid in expression, with a definitive insight—is it not found in this essay!]
Comment by Examiner and Examining Editor (jiantao) Xing 邢: [Based on the explanations of Cheng Yi 程頤 and Zhu Xi 朱熹, it threads them together with genuine understanding, conforming very well to the purport of the Classic.]
Comment by Examiner and Senior Compiler (xiuzhuan) Liu 劉: [Intimate personal comprehension that deeply grasps the meaning of the topic.]

Only when one is comprehensive in function is one sufficient to unite with principle. For excellence of assembly and benefitting things are functions manifested in affairs; ritual propriety and righteousness are principles inherent in the mind. Since the noble man who embodies the Creative (Qian 乾) is already comprehensive in function, how could he not be sufficient to unite with principle? In the Commentary on the Words of the Text (Wenyan 文言), the Sage explained the "flourishing" (heng 亨) and "advantage" (li 利) of the Creative and extended them to human affairs in this way.

If we consider it: ritual propriety is a principle inherent in the human mind. How, then, does the noble man practice ritual propriety? He causes all the cardinal guides and human relationships to fulfill their proper way, and every movement and deportment to hit the proper measure, so that among all the affairs in the world there is not a single one in which its excellence is not brought to perfection—this is what is meant by "excellence of assembly." Because the noble man's excellence of assembly is like this, what he treads in his conduct is entirely the measured pattern of Heavenly principle, and what his mind rests in is also the ceremonial rule of human…

text:
事之儀則豈不足以合禮乎禮而謂之合非勉强以
合之也蓋禮所以嘉會而嘉會即禮之見於用者也
若夫義者亦人心所具之理也君子之為義果何如
邪俾凡尊卑大小之各安其位洪纖高下之各適其
宜舉天下之物無一之不得其所焉是則所謂利物
矣君子之利物如此故泛應曲當者皆天理之所宜
曲成不遺者亦人心之裁制豈不足以和義乎義而
謂之和非矯揉以和之也蓋義所以利物而利物即
義之見於用者也曰嘉會曰利物非所謂周於用乎
===
曰合禮曰和義非所謂會夫理乎文言此節上文言
天德之自然而寓之於人者也君子體仁及此以下
則又言人事之當然也人能盡人事之當然則有以
合天德之自然故下文又曰君子行此四德者故曰
乾元亨利貞讀者宜合而觀之
在天成象在地成形變化見矣是故剛柔相摩
八卦相盪鼓之以雷霆潤之以風雨日月運
行一寒一暑乾道成男坤道成女
戴仁

punctuated:
事之儀則，豈不足以合禮乎？禮而謂之合，非勉强以合之也，蓋禮所以嘉會，而嘉會即禮之見於用者也。若夫義者，亦人心所具之理也。君子之為義，果何如邪？俾凡尊卑大小之各安其位，洪纖高下之各適其宜，舉天下之物無一之不得其所焉，是則所謂利物矣。君子之利物如此，故泛應曲當者，皆天理之所宜；曲成不遺者，亦人心之裁制，豈不足以和義乎？義而謂之和，非矯揉以和之也，蓋義所以利物，而利物即義之見於用者也。曰嘉會，曰利物，非所謂周於用乎？曰合禮，曰和義，非所謂會夫理乎？《文言》此節，上文言天德之自然而寓之於人者也；「君子體仁」及此以下，則又言人事之當然也。人能盡人事之當然，則有以合天德之自然，故下文又曰：「君子行此四德者，故曰：乾，元亨利貞。」讀者宜合而觀之。

在天成象，在地成形，變化見矣。是故剛柔相摩，八卦相盪，鼓之以雷霆，潤之以風雨，日月運行，一寒一暑，乾道成男，坤道成女。

戴仁
translation_en:
… models of human affairs—how then could this not be sufficient to conform to propriety (li)? Speaking of propriety in terms of "conforming" does not mean forcing oneself to conform to it; rather, propriety is that by which one makes the assemblage of excellences (jiahui), and making the assemblage of excellences is simply propriety manifested in function. As for righteousness (yi), it too is a principle inherent in the human mind. How, indeed, does the noble man practice righteousness? He ensures that the noble and base, the great and small, each rest securely in their positions, and that the vast and minute, the high and low, each suit what is appropriate to them, so that of all the things in the world there is not one that fails to find its proper place—this is what is called benefiting things (liwu). Because the noble man benefits things in this manner, his broad responses and intricate appropriateness are all what is fitting according to Heavenly principle, and his meticulous completion of things without omission is likewise the regulation of the human mind—how then could this not be sufficient to harmonize with righteousness? Speaking of righteousness in terms of "harmonizing" does not mean artificially bending oneself to harmonize with it; rather, righteousness is that by which one benefits things, and benefiting things is simply righteousness manifested in function. Calling it "making the assemblage of excellences" and "benefiting things"—is this not what is meant by being comprehensive in function? Calling it "conforming to propriety" and "harmonizing with righteousness"—is this not what is meant by converging with principle? In this section of the Commentary on the Words of the Text (Wenyan), the preceding lines speak of the naturalness of Heavenly virtue as it resides in human beings; from "the noble man embodies benevolence" down to this point and beyond, it speaks in turn of what ought to be done in human affairs. When a person can fully realize what ought to be done in human affairs, he is thereby able to conform to the naturalness of Heavenly virtue; therefore, the text below goes on to say: "The noble man practices these four virtues; therefore it is said: 'Qian: originating, flourishing, advantageous, and correct and firm.'" The reader ought to consider these parts together.

"In heaven, images are formed; on earth, shapes are formed; and thus changes and transformations are manifested. Therefore, the hard and the soft rub against each other, and the eight trigrams agitate one another. Things are roused by thunder and lightning, moistened by wind and rain; the sun and moon move in their courses, producing now cold, now heat; the way of Qian forms the male, and the way of Kun forms the female."

Dai Ren 戴仁

title: 天順六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官訓導潘批近時學易者詞尚奇僻而於本旨多泥而
不達此作能本朱子本義以為說發明孔子
作易之意殆無餘蘊詞義俱足次
同考試官教諭呉批作大傳題者多蹈襲陳言令人厭觀此作能
化腐為新足見筆力實易經中之翹楚者
考試官檢討邢批始終以實體言之允當允當
考試官脩撰劉批講造化易書之理明殆熟於易者
因陰陽之實體有以著乎易書推易書之變化有以
見於實體夫陰陽變化無往而不在也苟徒知實體
===
著於造化而不知實體具於易書又烏足以言易哉
蓋嘗觀之易書不外乎陰陽而陰陽不外乎變化方
易之未畫也則變化見於天地之象形焉觀夫天之
日月星辰之屬懸象以著明凡在於上者皆成象也
地之山川動植之屬流峙而生成凡在於下者皆成形
也成象屬乎陽而易中蓍策卦爻之陰變為陽者於
此而可見矣成形屬乎陰而易中蓍策卦爻之陽化
為陰者於此而可見矣所謂因陰陽之實體有以著
乎易書者如此至若易之既畫也則變化又有以成

蓋嘗觀之易書不外乎陰陽而陰陽不外乎變化方
易之未畫也則變化見於天地之象形焉觀夫天之

爲陰者於此而可見矣所謂因陰陽之實體有以著
乎易書者如此至若易之既畫也則變化又有以成
punctuated:
同考試官訓導潘批：近時學《易》者詞尚奇僻，而於本旨多泥而不達。此作能本朱子《本義》以為說，發明孔子作《易》之意，殆無餘蘊，詞義俱足。次。
同考試官教諭呉批：作《大傳》題者，多蹈襲陳言，令人厭觀。此作能化腐為新，足見筆力，實《易經》中之翹楚者。
考試官檢討邢批：始終以實體言之，允當，允當。
考試官脩撰劉批：講造化《易》書之理明，殆熟於《易》者。
因陰陽之實體有以著乎《易》書，推《易》書之變化有以見於實體。夫陰陽變化，無往而不在也。苟徒知實體著於造化，而不知實體具於《易》書，又烏足以言《易》哉？蓋嘗觀之：《易》書不外乎陰陽，而陰陽不外乎變化。方《易》之未畫也，則變化見於天地之象形焉。觀夫天之日月星辰之屬，懸象以著明，凡在於上者皆成象也；地之山川動植之屬，流峙而生成，凡在於下者皆成形也。成象屬乎陽，而《易》中蓍策卦爻之陰變為陽者，於此而可見矣；成形屬乎陰，而《易》中蓍策卦爻之陽化為陰者，於此而可見矣。所謂「因陰陽之實體有以著乎《易》書」者如此。至若《易》之既畫也，則變化又有以成
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner Assistant Instructor Pan: "In recent times, those who study the Book of Changes (Yi) favor strange and obscure phrasing in their words, yet with regard to the fundamental meaning they are mostly bogged down and fail to grasp it. This essay is able to base its argument on Master Zhu's Original Meaning of the Book of Changes (Benyi), elucidating Confucius's intention in composing the commentaries on the Changes while leaving almost nothing unexpressed. Both its diction and its meaning are sufficient. Second rank."

Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Wu: "Those who write on topics from the Great Commentary (Dazhuan) mostly tread in and repeat stale words, making them tiresome to read. This essay is able to transform the stale into the new, which is enough to show the strength of its brush. Truly, he is an outstanding figure among the candidates in the Classic of Changes (Yijing)."

Comment by Examiner Examining Editor Xing: "From beginning to end he speaks of it in terms of concrete substance. Truly fitting, truly fitting."

Comment by Examiner Senior Compiler Liu: "His explanation of the principles of cosmic creation and the Book of Changes is clear; he is doubtless someone thoroughly versed in the Changes."

On the basis of the concrete substance of yin and yang, there is that by which transformations are made manifest in the Book of Changes; by extending the transformations and changes of the Book of Changes, there is that by which they are seen in concrete substance. Now, yin and yang, transformation and change, are present everywhere. If one merely knows that concrete substance is manifest in cosmic creation, yet does not know that concrete substance is contained within the Book of Changes, how then is one qualified to speak of the Changes?

I have observed that the Book of Changes does not go beyond yin and yang, and yin and yang do not go beyond transformation and change. When the trigrams of the Changes had not yet been drawn, transformation and change were seen in the images and forms of heaven and earth. Looking at such things of heaven as the sun, moon, stars, and constellations, which suspend their images to shine forth brightly—all things that are above form images; and such things of earth as mountains, rivers, animals, and plants, which flow, stand lofty, come into being, and grow—all things that are below form physical shapes. Forming images pertains to yang, and that by which yin transforms into yang in the yarrow stalks, hexagrams, and lines within the Changes can be seen right here; forming physical shapes pertains to yin, and that by which yang changes into yin in the yarrow stalks, hexagrams, and lines within the Changes can be seen right here. Such is what is meant by "on the basis of the concrete substance of yin and yang, there is that by which transformations are made manifest in the Book of Changes." As for when the trigrams of the Changes had already been drawn, transformation and change in turn had that by which they formed…

title: 天順六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
夫象形焉是故卦畫之初剛柔兩畫而已兩相摩而
為四四相摩而為八八相盪而為六十四則變化不
窮而生生不已此則易卦之變化也由是震離相交
而坎巽相次則雷霆鼓而風雨潤離坎相推而乾坤
相易則日月運而寒暑行此變化之成象也非即在
天之成象乎由是坤索乎乾而得震坎艮之三男乾
索乎坤而得巽離兌之三女此變化之成形也非即
在地之成形乎所謂推易書之變化有以見於實體
者又如此大抵易以道陰陽而已大傳此章言天尊地
===
卑而至變化見者乃舉造化以明易也言剛柔相摩
而至於成男成女者乃舉易以明造化也然皆不外
乎陰陽而已易與造化夫豈二乎哉
書義
侯以明之
何恂
同考試官訓導許批此題本難發揮獨此篇措辭不苟反覆議
論深得帝舜以禮為教之意置之パ前列孰
曰不宜

punctuated:
夫象形焉。是故卦畫之初，剛柔兩畫而已。兩相摩而為四，四相摩而為八，八相盪而為六十四，則變化不窮而生生不已，此則易卦之變化也。由是震離相交而坎巽相次，則雷霆鼓而風雨潤；離坎相推而乾坤相易，則日月運而寒暑行，此變化之成象也，非即在天之成象乎？由是坤索乎乾而得震、坎、艮之三男，乾索乎坤而得巽、離、兌之三女，此變化之成形也，非即在地之成形乎？所謂推易書之變化有以見於實體者又如此。大抵《易》以道陰陽而已。《大傳》此章言「天尊地卑」而至「變化見」者，乃舉造化以明《易》也；言「剛柔相摩」而至於「成男」、「成女」者，乃舉《易》以明造化也。然皆不外乎陰陽而已，《易》與造化，夫豈二乎哉？

書義

侯以明之。
何恂
同考試官訓導許批：此題本難發揮，獨此篇措辭不苟，反覆議論，深得帝舜以禮為教之意。置之パ前列，孰曰不宜？
translation_en:
…the celestial images and terrestrial forms. Therefore, at the beginning of the drawing of the hexagrams, there were only the two lines of the firm and the yielding. The two rubbed against each other to become four; the four rubbed against each other to become eight; the eight agitated against one another to become sixty-four—thus transformations and changes are inexhaustible, and generation after generation never ceases. This, then, is the transformation and change of the hexagrams of the Book of Changes (Yi 易). From this, Zhen 震 and Li 離 intersect while Kan 坎 and Xun 巽 follow in sequence, and thus thunder and lightning rouse things while wind and rain moisten them; Li and Kan push each other forward while Qian 乾 and Kun 坤 alternate with each other, and thus the sun and moon revolve while cold and heat proceed. This is how transformation and change form images—is it not precisely the forming of images in Heaven? From this, Kun seeks from Qian and obtains the three sons—Zhen, Kan, and Gen 艮—while Qian seeks from Kun and obtains the three daughters—Xun, Li, and Dui 兌. This is how transformation and change form physical shapes—is it not precisely the forming of physical shapes on Earth? What is meant by extending the transformations and changes of the Book of Changes so as to see them in substantive reality is, again, like this. In general, the Book of Changes simply speaks of yin and yang. When this chapter of the Great Commentary (Dazhuan 大傳) speaks of "Heaven is lofty and Earth is low" down to "transformations and changes appear," it cites the creative processes of nature to elucidate the Book of Changes; when it speaks of "the firm and the yielding rub against each other" down to "forming the male" and "forming the female," it cites the Book of Changes to elucidate the creative processes of nature. Yet all of this goes no further than yin and yang. How could the Book of Changes and the creative processes of nature be two different things?

Exposition on the Book of Documents (Shu yi 書義)

"The target to distinguish them."
By He Xun 何恂.
Comment by Associate Examiner Assistant Instructor Xu 許: This topic is inherently difficult to elaborate upon, yet this essay alone is meticulous in its wording and argues the point back and forth, deeply grasping Emperor Shun's 舜 intention of using ritual to instruct. Placing it in the [?] forefront, who would say it is inappropriate?

title: 天順六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭譚批場中作此題者詞多艱澁惟此篇語新文暢
非學充才富者不能表而出之允以為當
考試官檢討邢批通篇以教為說不悖蔡傳
考試官脩撰劉批得聖人以禮為教之意
舉觀德之藝而明夫不善之人此聖人以禮為教也
夫不善之人在所當棄而聖人猶舉觀德之藝以明
之其以禮為教而不輕於棄人也為何如哉在昔帝
舜之時四方風動萬邦咸寧雖有庶頑讒說之不忠
不直棄而不教似無害於治者舜之心則以為天下
===
無不可化之人人亦無自絕於為善之理乃命伯禹
明之以射侯焉明之何如蓋欲驗其果頑讒與否也
射侯之禮本以觀德頑讒之人何有於德哉舜之舉
此蓋將以寓夫旌別之典所謂以禮為教也夫射之
中否判於此而人之善惡分於此故當射禮方行之
時彼所謂庶頑者甘心於庶頑則已使其有向善之
心也内焉必正其志外焉必直其體持弓引滿發而
中焉謂之有德可也否則雖滿鏃叩弦决無中鵠之
能其於德也何取是其為庶頑也果矣彼所謂讒說

考試官脩撰劉批：得聖人以禮為教之意。
舉觀德之藝而明夫不善之人，此聖人以禮為教也。夫不善之人在所當棄，而聖人猶舉觀德之藝以明之，其以禮為教而不輕於棄人也為何如哉！在昔帝舜之時，四方風動，萬邦咸寧，雖有庶頑讒說之不忠不直，棄而不教，似無害於治者。舜之心則以為天下無不可化之人，人亦無自絕於為善之理，乃命伯禹明之以射侯焉。明之何如？蓋欲驗其果頑讒與否也。射侯之禮，本以觀德，頑讒之人，何有於德哉？舜之舉此，蓋將以寓夫旌別之典，所謂以禮為教也。夫射之中否判於此，而人之善惡分於此。故當射禮方行之時，彼所謂庶頑者，甘心於庶頑則已；使其有向善之心也，内焉必正其志，外焉必直其體，持弓引滿，發而中焉，謂之有德可也；否則雖滿鏃叩弦，决無中鵠之能，其於德也何取？是其為庶頑也果矣。彼所謂讒說
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Instructor Tan's comment: Among those who wrote on this topic in the examination hall, the wording was mostly labored and obscure; only this essay has fresh language and a fluent style, which none could achieve without ample learning and rich talent. To single it out and present it is truly fitting.
Examiner Investigating Editor Xing's comment: The entire essay takes moral instruction as its thesis and does not conflict with Cai's Commentary.
Examiner Senior Compiler Liu's comment: It captures the sage's intention of using ritual as moral instruction.

To employ the art by which virtue is observed in order to distinguish those who are not good—this is how the sage used ritual as moral instruction. Now, people who are not good ought by rights to be cast aside, yet the sage still employed the art by which virtue is observed in order to distinguish them; how great indeed was his use of ritual as moral instruction and his reluctance to cast people aside lightly! In antiquity, in the time of Emperor Shun, the four quarters were moved as by the wind and the myriad states were all at peace; even though there were the obstinate and the slanderers who were disloyal and dishonest, to cast them aside without instructing them would have seemed no detriment to good order. Yet in his heart Shun considered that in all the world there is no person who cannot be transformed, and that no person has reason to cut himself off from doing good; therefore he commanded Boyu to distinguish them by means of the archery target. How did it distinguish them? It was to test whether they were truly obstinate and slanderous or not. The ritual of the archery target was originally meant for observing virtue; what virtue could obstinate and slanderous people possess? Shun instituted this because he intended to lodge within it the canon for distinguishing the good from the bad—what is meant by using ritual as moral instruction. Now whether a shot hits or misses is determined here, and whether a person is good or evil is divided here. Therefore, at the moment when the archery ritual is being performed, as for those called the obstinate, if they are content to remain obstinate, there is nothing more to be said; but if they have a mind inclined toward goodness, inwardly they will surely rectify their intentions and outwardly they will surely straighten their posture, grasping the bow and drawing it to the full, releasing the arrow and hitting the mark—and then they may be called virtuous. Otherwise, even if they draw the arrowhead to the full and nock it to the string, they will certainly lack the ability to hit the bull's-eye; what virtue is there to be found in them? Then their being obstinate is proved indeed. As for those called slanderers…

title: 天順六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
者甘心於讒說則已使其有遷善之念也其容體必
欲比於禮其節奏必欲比於樂持弓審固發而中焉
謂之有德可也否則雖張弓挾矢必無中的之巧其
於德也何觀此其為讒說也審矣一射禮之講而人
之不善者亦有所化焉此聖人以禮為教而非後世
之所能及也歟噫斯旨也即成周之考藝在於秋合
射之後也雖其所考者在國子非可以與有虞之頑
讒例論然觀德以射則一而已毋容以差殊觀
天齊于民俾我一日非終惟終在人

title: 天順六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
公夫刑由上天之所立法必因罪而異施一至公之
道耳則夫王者之告同姓諸侯得不舉之以為言哉
昔穆王訓刑之意若曰五刑之設非人君所恃以為
治也盖天以是而整乎民之不治者于焉以服民心
而率於治化之中使我為一日之用以輔治之所不
及耳五罰之設亦非人君所恃以為威也盖天以是
而齊乎民之不一者于焉以棐民彝而歸於德教之
内俾我為暫時之用以弼教之所未備耳然主刑雖
在於君而服刑則在乎民如人或無意而罹於刑也
===
我則核實其罪無簡不聽而輕以宥之焉其輕也特
視乎人之所犯何如耳非我所得而輕也人或有意
而犯乎法也我則惟察惟法其審克之而重以刑之
焉其重也亦視夫人之所犯何如耳非我所得而重
也是則刑出于天而為君所用罪係乎人而非君所
私穆王以是為言何其忠厚之至哉雖然吕刑一書
專為訓刑而作觀其所載曰今天相民曰天齊于民
以見刑之所自出者天也曰朕敬于刑曰俾我一日
以見刑之所以用者君也自然之理出於天而當然

… impartiality. Now, punishments are established by High Heaven, and the law must be applied differently according to the offense; it is simply the Way of utmost impartiality. Then, when a true king instructs the feudal lords of the same surname, how could he not raise these points in his words?

In antiquity, the meaning of King Mu's instruction on punishments was as if to say: The establishment of the Five Punishments is not what a ruler relies upon to govern. Rather, Heaven uses them to bring order to those among the people who are unruly, thereby winning the submission of the people's hearts and leading them into the midst of orderly transformation, granting me their use for a single day merely to supplement where governance falls short. The establishment of the Five Fines is likewise not what a ruler relies upon to project awe. Rather, Heaven uses them to make uniform those among the people who are not unified, thereby aiding the people's constant norms and bringing them back within moral instruction, granting me their temporary use merely to assist where instruction is not yet complete.

Yet although presiding over punishments rests with the ruler, incurring punishments rests with the people. If someone unintentionally falls foul of the punishments, I then verify the facts of his offense—where there is no verifiable proof, the case is not heard—and lightly pardon him; this lightness depends solely on the nature of what the person has committed, and is not something that I can make light on my own. If someone intentionally violates the law, I then examine carefully and follow the law, investigating thoroughly before heavily punishing him; this heaviness likewise depends on the nature of what the person has committed, and is not something that I can make heavy on my own.

Thus, punishments originate from Heaven and are employed by the ruler, while offenses depend on the person and are not subject to the ruler's personal bias. That King Mu spoke in these terms—how supremely magnanimous and compassionate! Even so, the chapterPunishments of Lü (Lü xing) was composed specifically to instruct on punishments. Looking at what is recorded in it, it says "Today Heaven aids the people" and "Heaven brings uniformity to the people," to show that the source from which punishments originate is Heaven; and it says "I am reverent toward punishments" and "granting me for a single day," to show that the one by whom punishments are employed is the ruler. 下之法是以普天率土非一姓也莫不愛戴武王以
為天子而所以應之者維以順德焉群黎百姓非一
人也靡不親媚武王以為元后而所以化之者亦維
以順德焉盖順德即孝也武王長言孝思而天下化
於孝是能以一人之孝為千萬人之孝其孝之昭然
能嗣其先世之事者不可掩矣以一身之德為天下
之德其孝之明哉能繼其先王之緒者不可昧矣武
王之道昭明如此為後王者苟能繼其迹而愈光焉
又豈不獲乎福哉是故法武王之信必天命之永配
===
而無頃刻之或違可也法武王之孝必世德之是求
而無一息之敢忘可也誠如是將見雖於萬斯年之
久子子孫孫亦永荷天祿而不替所謂邦國是有者
有焉雖萬有千歲之遠本支百世亦允獲天眷而無
窮所謂百祿是遒者有焉噫繼三后於已往開後嗣
於方来非武王之達孝其孰能如是哉抑下武一詩
所以詠嘆武王者不一而足要之武王之道不過信
與孝爾故於此又即其孝之著者以勉其後人然武
王之孝豈一朝一夕暫行復輟者所能至哉必常永

punctuated: 下之法。是以普天率土，非一姓也，莫不愛戴武王以為天子，而所以應之者，維以順德焉；群黎百姓，非一人也，靡不親媚武王以為元后，而所以化之者，亦維以順德焉。盖順德即孝也。武王長言孝思，而天下化於孝，是能以一人之孝為千萬人之孝，其孝之昭然能嗣其先世之事者，不可掩矣；以一身之德為天下之德，其孝之明哉能繼其先王之緒者，不可昧矣。武王之道昭明如此，為後王者，苟能繼其迹而愈光焉，又豈不獲乎福哉？是故法武王之信，必天命之永配而無頃刻之或違可也；法武王之孝，必世德之是求而無一息之敢忘可也。誠如是，將見雖於萬斯年之久，子子孫孫亦永荷天祿而不替，所謂「邦國是有」者有焉；雖萬有千歲之遠，本支百世亦允獲天眷而無窮，所謂「百祿是遒」者有焉。噫！繼三后於已往，開後嗣於方来，非武王之達孝，其孰能如是哉？抑《下武》一詩，所以詠嘆武王者不一而足，要之武王之道，不過信與孝爾。故於此又即其孝之著者，以勉其後人。然武王之孝，豈一朝一夕、暫行復輟者所能至哉？必常永
translation_en: … model for the entire world. Therefore, across all under Heaven and within the bounds of the land, there was not just a single clan, yet none failed to love and revere King Wu as the Son of Heaven, and that by which they responded to him was solely through compliant virtue; among the multitude of the common people and the hundred surnames, there was not just a single person, yet none failed to feel affection and devotion toward King Wu as their supreme sovereign, and that by which they were transformed by him was likewise solely through compliant virtue. For compliant virtue is none other than filial piety. King Wu constantly spoke of filial thoughts, and the world was transformed by filial piety. Thus, he was able to make the filial piety of one man become the filial piety of tens of millions; that his filial piety was so illustrious as to succeed to the undertakings of his ancestors could not be concealed! He made the virtue of his single person become the virtue of the entire world; how brilliant was his filial piety, and that it could continue the enterprise of the former kings could not be obscured! Since the Way of King Wu was so illustrious and bright, if later kings can follow in his footsteps and make them shine ever more brightly, how could they fail to obtain blessings? Therefore, in emulating the trustworthiness of King Wu, they must forever match the Mandate of Heaven without violating it for even an instant; in emulating the filial piety of King Wu, they must seek the hereditary virtue of their house without daring to forget it for even a single breath. If it is truly so, one shall see that even through the long duration of ten thousand years, sons and grandsons will forever bear the blessings of Heaven without decline—what the Ode calls "possessing the states and territories" will be realized therein; even into the distant future of ten thousand and a thousand years, the main line and collateral branches for a hundred generations will truly receive the favor of Heaven without end—what the Ode calls "gathering the hundred blessings" will be realized therein. Alas! Continuing the work of the Three Sovereigns in the past and opening the way for descendants in the future—without the far-reaching filial piety of King Wu, who could have accomplished such as this? Furthermore, in the ode "Xia wu," the ways in which King Wu is praised in song are not merely one, yet in essence the Way of King Wu is nothing more than trustworthiness and filial piety. Hence, at this point the poet again takes up the manifest renown of his filial piety in order to encourage his descendants. text:
不已盡誠無間而後可庶幾也此又讀者之所當知
在彼無惡在此無斁庶幾夙夜以永終譽
二美

惟能得人心而無間，斯可保聲譽於無窮。夫人欲保其聲譽者固難，而得人心則保聲譽之本也。王者於先代之後而以是勉之，其欲脩德以保譽之意為何如哉！昔杞、宋二國助祭於周，周人作詩，謂夫爾二王之後，来助祭於我周也，我既尊之曰「客」，以罄其敬待之心；比之以「鷺」，以見爾脩整之容矣。然爾之有此譽也，豈可不思有以保全於無窮哉？其必在彼封國也，質爾人民，謹爾侯度，俾民有所倚賴而無憎惡之心；
translation_en:
…ceaselessly and exhaust one's sincerity without interruption before one can hope to approximate it. This too is what the reader ought to know.

"There, there is no dislike; here, there is no weariness. So may they be day and night, to perpetuate their final fame!"
Er Mei
Associate Examiner Instructor Xiao [comment: This ode is the Zhou king's encouragement to the descendants of the two preceding dynasties. Most writers compose words of pure praise, which completely misses the original intent. Only this essay grasps the meaning genuinely and incisively, with a torrential flow of the brush; he is truly a scholar of learning.]
Associate Examiner Instructor Wang [comment: The brush-strength of this essay is vigorous and ancient, towering like the peaks of Mount Tai and Mount Hua, emerging layer upon layer. Could anyone not deeply versed in the Classics speak of it like this? High recommendation is truly fitting.]
Examiner Examining Editor Xing [comment: The diction and tone are calm and dignified, bringing out the loyal and generous spirit of the poet. Praiseworthy.]
Examiner Senior Compiler Liu [comment: It captures the purport of gentle and sincere thickness of character.]

Only by winning the hearts of the people without interruption can one preserve one's reputation forever. Now, for a person to preserve his reputation is certainly difficult, and winning the hearts of the people is the root of preserving one's reputation. When the true king encouraged the descendants of the former dynasties with this, how deep was his desire that they cultivate their virtue in order to preserve their fame! In the past, when the two states of Qi and Song assisted at the sacrifices in Zhou, the people of Zhou composed this ode, saying: You descendants of the two former kings have come to assist at the sacrifices in our Zhou. We have already honored you with the title of "guests" to exhaust our heart of respectful treatment, and compared you to "egrets" to show your well-ordered and dignified bearing. Yet since you possess this fame, how could you not think of a way to preserve it intact forever? Surely, when you are there in your enfeoffed states, you must bring stability to your people and carefully observe your feudal measures, so that the people have something to rely upon and harbor no feelings of dislike; …

title: 天順六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
纘乃舊服無忝祖考使人有所親愛而無疾棄之意
可也其必在此王國也淑愼爾止不愆于儀有以為
人之瞻仰而人無或厭愼乃服命率由典常有以為
人之崇重而人無或斁可也爾既能得人心如此將
見自今以往尊之為我客則人將不以我為溢美爾
庶幾夙夜無間得以保此聲譽於無窮焉比之以振
鷺則人將不謂汝為過情爾庶幾朝夕不懈得以長
有此聲譽於後日焉謂之以永終譽吾知其令聞之
施愈遠而益隆聲譽之著愈久而不替矣吁王者於
===
先代之後不惟勉之切而又望之深其忠厚之意何
其至哉抑考杞宋二國乃夏殷之後周人以客禮遇
之者也故其來助祭也敬愛之心勸勉之意無所不
至書微子之命亦曰與國咸休又曰俾我有周無斁
合而觀之則有周公平正大愛人以德氣象可見矣
春秋義
蔡人衛人陳人從王伐鄭〔桓公五年〕遂會晉侯齊侯
宋公衛侯鄭伯曹伯邾人滕人伐秦〔成公十三年〕
程宏

之者也故其來助祭也敬愛之心勸勉之意無所不

宋公衛侯鄭伯曹伯邾人滕人伐秦〔成公十三年〕

punctuated:
纘乃舊服，無忝祖考，使人有所親愛而無疾棄之意可也。其必在此王國也，淑愼爾止，不愆于儀，有以為人之瞻仰而人無或厭；愼乃服命，率由典常，有以為人之崇重而人無或斁可也。爾既能得人心如此，將見自今以往，尊之為我客，則人將不以我為溢美，爾庶幾夙夜無間，得以保此聲譽於無窮焉；比之以振鷺，則人將不謂汝為過情，爾庶幾朝夕不懈，得以長有此聲譽於後日焉。謂之「以永終譽」，吾知其令聞之施，愈遠而益隆，聲譽之著，愈久而不替矣。吁！王者於先代之後，不惟勉之切而又望之深，其忠厚之意何其至哉！抑考杞、宋二國，乃夏、殷之後，周人以客禮遇之者也。故其來助祭也，敬愛之心，勸勉之意，無所不至。《書·微子之命》亦曰：「與國咸休。」又曰：「俾我有周無斁。」合而觀之，則有周公平正大、愛人以德氣象可見矣。

春秋義
蔡人、衛人、陳人從王伐鄭〔桓公五年〕；遂會晉侯、齊侯、宋公、衛侯、鄭伯、曹伯、邾人、滕人伐秦〔成公十三年〕。
程宏
translation_en:
…continue your ancient duties and bring no shame upon your ancestors, causing people to feel affection for you without any thought of loathing or abandoning you—that will do. And surely, while you are here in this royal kingdom, if you are virtuous and cautious in your demeanor and commit no fault in your deportment, giving people cause to look up to you without anyone ever growing weary of you; and if you are careful of your robes and charge and follow the constant norms, giving people cause to hold you in high esteem without anyone ever tiring of you—that will do. Once you are able to win people's hearts in this way, it will be seen that from now on, when we honor you as our guests, people will not consider us to be offering excessive praise, and you may perhaps, day and night without interruption, preserve this reputation forever; and when we compare you to a flock of egrets in flight, people will not say that you are receiving undeserved acclaim, and you may perhaps, morning and evening without slackening, long possess this reputation in days to come. When the ode says, "thus to perpetuate their fame forever," I know that the reach of their good renown will grow ever more distant and lofty, and the brilliance of their reputation will endure ever longer without decline. Ah! Toward the descendants of former dynasties, the true king not only exhorted them earnestly but also placed deep hopes in them—how consummate was his generous and magnanimous intent! Moreover, if we examine the two states of Qi and Song, they were the descendants of Xia and Yin, whom the Zhou people treated with the rites due to guests. Therefore, when they came to assist in the sacrifices, there was no limit to the feelings of respect and affection and the intent to encourage and exhort them. In the Book of Documents, "The Charge to the Viscount of Wei" (Weizi zhi ming) likewise says, "Sharing in the auspiciousness of the state," and again, "Causing our House of Zhou never to grow weary of you." Viewed together, the fair, upright, and magnanimous spirit of the House of Zhou in loving others through virtue can clearly be seen.

Expositions on the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

Cheng Hong 程宏

text:
同考試官訓導鄭批作者多知上截變以而書從少知下截變从以
書會此卷段落分明措詞典雅得聖人尊君
抑臣之旨矣
考試官檢討邢批以聖人書法為主意最是
考試官脩撰劉批以尊君抑臣立論合經旨
王室以諸侯討罪春秋既變文以著尊君之義諸侯
從王臣討强春秋復變文以示抑臣之權夫桓王率
諸侯則書從諸侯從劉成則書會春秋正名分之意
為何如哉慨自周轍既東侯度日肆王室之不尊也
===
久矣有如桓王在位怒鄭伯之不朝率三國以致討
雖曰躬率諸侯嚴號令於桓武之國而無以服鄭伯之
抗衡雖曰親冒矢石施天討於不臣之邦而無以止
祝聃之逆節故傳稱王以諸侯伐鄭其與宋以四國
伐鄭無異矣聖人脩經至此意謂周室雖衰非可與
列國等也故變文書三國從王伐鄭示君行而臣從
也非所以著尊君之義乎自是而後王室益微臣職
之有乖也甚矣有如晋厲世伯憾秦人之不道從劉
成以致伐徒知陳師鞠旅奮威武於西戎之境而不

抑臣之旨矣

諸侯則書從諸侯從劉歲則書會春秋正名分之意
爲何如哉慨自周轍既東侯度日肆王室之不尊也
===
久矣有如桓王在位怒鄭伯之不朝率三國以致討
辭曰從率諸侯嚴號令於桓武之國而無以辭鄭伯之
抗衡卿曰觀冒矢石施天討於不庭之所而無以止
視聽之逆節故傳稱王以諸侯伐鄭書與宋以四國
伐鄭無異矣聖人脩經至此意謂周室雖衰非可與
列國等也故變文書三國從王伐鄭示君行而臣從
也非所以著尊君之義乎自是而後王室益微臣職
之有乖也甚矣有如晉厲世伯憾秦人之不道從劉
成以致伐徒知陳師鞠旅奮威武於西戎之境而不
punctuated:
同考試官訓導鄭批：作者多知上截變「以」而書「從」，少知下截變「从」以書「會」。此卷段落分明，措詞典雅，得聖人尊君抑臣之旨矣。
考試官檢討邢批：以聖人書法為主，意最是。
考試官脩撰劉批：以尊君抑臣立論，合經旨。
王室以諸侯討罪，《春秋》既變文以著尊君之義；諸侯從王臣討强，《春秋》復變文以示抑臣之權。夫桓王率諸侯則書「從」，諸侯從劉成則書「會」，《春秋》正名分之意為何如哉！
慨自周轍既東，侯度日肆，王室之不尊也久矣。有如桓王在位，怒鄭伯之不朝，率三國以致討。雖曰躬率諸侯，嚴號令於桓、武之國，而無以服鄭伯之抗衡；雖曰親冒矢石，施天討於不臣之邦，而無以止祝聃之逆節。故傳稱「王以諸侯伐鄭」，其與宋以四國伐鄭無異矣。聖人脩經至此，意謂周室雖衰，非可與列國等也。故變文書「三國從王伐鄭」，示君行而臣從也，非所以著尊君之義乎？
自是而後，王室益微，臣職之有乖也甚矣。有如晋厲世伯，憾秦人之不道，從劉成以致伐。徒知陳師鞠旅，奮威武於西戎之境，而不

Comment by Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Zheng: Most writers know that the first part alters the word "use" (yi 以) to record "follow" (cong 從), while few know that the second part alters "follow" (cong 从) to record "join" (hui 會). This paper has clear structure and elegant diction; it has grasped the Sage's purport of honoring the ruler and restraining the subjects.
Comment by Examiner and Examining Editor Xing: Taking the Sage's historiographical method as the central theme, its meaning is most sound.
Comment by Examiner and Senior Compiler Liu: It builds its argument on honoring the ruler and restraining the subjects, which accords with the purport of the Classic.
When the royal house used the feudal lords to punish an offender, the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) altered the wording in order to make manifest the principle of honoring the ruler; when the feudal lords followed the king's ministers to punish a powerful state, the Spring and Autumn Annals again altered the wording in order to demonstrate the authority of restraining subjects. Now, when King Huan led the feudal lords, it recorded that they "followed" (cong) him; when the feudal lords followed Liu and Cheng, it recorded that they "joined" (hui) in a meeting. How profound indeed was the intention of the Spring and Autumn Annals in rectifying names and statuses!
Alas, ever since the chariot tracks of Zhou moved east, the conduct of the feudal lords grew daily more unbridled, and the royal house had long ceased to be honored! Take the case of King Huan on the throne: angered that the Earl of Zheng did not come to court, he led three states to carry out a punitive expedition. Although one might say he personally led the feudal lords to enforce strict commands upon the state founded by Dukes Huan and Wu of Zheng, he had no means to subdue the defiance of the Earl of Zheng; although one might say he personally braved arrows and stones to inflict Heaven's punishment upon an unsubmissive state, he had no means to halt the rebellious outrage of Zhu Dan. Therefore the Zuo Commentary states that "the King used (yi) the feudal lords to attack Zheng," which was no different from Song using four states to attack Zheng. When the Sage compiled the Classic and reached this point, his thought was that although the House of Zhou had declined, it could not be placed on a par with the various feudal states. Therefore he altered the wording to record that the three states "followed the King to attack Zheng," showing that when the ruler marches, the subjects follow. Was this not the way to make manifest the principle of honoring the ruler?
From this time onward, the royal house grew ever weaker, and the breach of subjects' duties became extreme! Take the case of Duke Li of Jin, a hereditary hegemon: resenting the waylessness of the men of Qin, he followed Liu and Cheng to carry out an attack. He merely knew how to array his armies and address his troops, displaying martial might along the borders of the Western Rong, while not…

title: 天順六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
□侯不可以俯從王臣徒知稱戈比干旅兵力於
亂民之邦而不知王臣不可以統合列國故傳稱公
會諸侯從劉成伐秦其與三國從王伐鄭無異矣聖
人脩經至此意謂劉成雖貴非可與至尊比也故變
文書遂會諸侯伐秦若劉成無與焉者非所以示抑
臣之權乎吁以天子而以諸侯則變文而書從以諸
侯而從王臣則變文而書會春秋於名分之際嚴矣
雖然伐秦之役固不足論伐鄭之舉君子不能無慨
焉戰于繻葛而不書戰王卒大敗而不書敗春秋所
===
以存天下之防也是故伐鄭不服而後王命不行於
天下至使諸侯大夫得以專盟會征伐之柄未必不
由此以啓之也讀經至此不能不為之三嘆

□侯不可以俯從王臣；徒知稱戈比干，旅兵力於亂民之邦，而不知王臣不可以統合列國。故傳稱「公會諸侯從劉成伐秦」，其與「三國從王伐鄭」無異矣。聖人脩經至此，意謂劉成雖貴，非可與至尊比也；故變文書「遂會諸侯伐秦」，若劉成無與焉者，非所以示抑臣之權乎？吁！以天子而以諸侯，則變文而書「從」；以諸侯而從王臣，則變文而書「會」。《春秋》於名分之際嚴矣。雖然，伐秦之役固不足論，伐鄭之舉，君子不能無慨焉。戰于繻葛而不書戰，王卒大敗而不書敗，《春秋》所以存天下之防也。是故伐鄭不服，而後王命不行於天下，至使諸侯、大夫得以專盟會征伐之柄，未必不由此以啓之也。讀經至此，不能不為之三嘆。

楚子、陳侯、鄭伯盟于辰陵〔宣公十一年〕；公及楚人、秦人、宋人、陳人、衛人、鄭人、齊人、曹人、邾人、薛人、鄫人盟于蜀〔成公二年〕；叔孫豹會晉趙武、楚屈建、蔡公孫歸生、衛石惡、陳孔奐、鄭良霄、許人、曹人于宋〔襄公二十七年〕；叔孫豹會晉趙武、楚公子圍、齊國弱、宋向戌、衛齊惡、陳公子招、蔡公孫歸
translation_en:
… [know that?] feudal lords cannot stoop to follow the King's ministers; he only knew to raise halberds and join shields, marshaling military force in the land of rebellious people, without knowing that the King's ministers cannot unite and command the various states. Therefore, the Commentary states that "the Duke met the feudal lords to follow Liu Cheng [Su of Liu, 劉康公] in attacking Qin," which is no different in phrasing from "the three states followed the King in attacking Zheng." When the Sage edited the Classic at this point, his meaning was that although Liu Cheng was of noble rank, he could not be compared with the Supreme Sovereign; therefore, he altered the wording and wrote "thereupon met the feudal lords to attack Qin," as if Liu Cheng had taken no part in it—is this not how he demonstrated the curtailing of a minister's authority? Alas! When the Son of Heaven employs the feudal lords, the wording is altered to write "followed"; when the feudal lords follow the King's ministers, the wording is altered to write "met." The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) is strict indeed regarding the boundaries of status and duty! Even so, while the campaign against Qin is certainly not worth discussing, the gentleman cannot help feeling a sigh of regret over the expedition against Zheng. That they fought at Xuge and yet the battle is not recorded, and that the King's troops suffered a great defeat and yet the defeat is not recorded—this is how the Spring and Autumn Annals preserves the moral bulwarks of the realm. Therefore, after Zheng was attacked and did not submit, the King's commands were no longer carried out in the world, eventually allowing the feudal lords and grandees to monopolize the authority over covenants, assemblies, and punitive expeditions—which was not necessarily not initiated by this very event. Reading the Classic to this point, one cannot help sighing over it repeatedly.

The Viscount of Chu, the Marquis of Chen, and the Earl of Zheng made a covenant at Chenling [11th year of Duke Xuan]; the Duke and men of Chu, Qin, Song, Chen, Wei, Zheng, Qi, Cao, Zhu, Xue, and Zeng made a covenant at Shu [2nd year of Duke Cheng]; Shusun Bao met Zhao Wu of Jin, Qu Jian of Chu, Gongsun Guisheng of Cai, Shi E of Wei, Kong Huan of Chen, Liang Xiao of Zheng, a man of Xu, and a man of Cao at Song [27th year of Duke Xiang]; Shusun Bao met Zhao Wu of Jin, Gongzi Wei of Chu, Guo Ruo of Qi, Xiang Xu of Song, Qi E of Wei, Gongzi Zhao of Chen, Gongsun Gui…

title: 天順六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
生鄭罕虎許人曹人于虢〔昭公元年〕公會晉侯及
吳子于黄池〔哀公十三年〕
程宏
同考試官訓導鄭批塲中作此題者多昧本旨間能知之而又不能
發唯此卷經旨詳明措詞雄健非熟於
麟經者不能也
考試官檢討邢批春秋於內外名實之分甚嚴此作能發揮
之是可尚也
考試官脩撰劉批聖人謹名實之辨正以內夏外夷此作得之矣
===
盟會迭講於內外春秋始紀其實而終正其名好會
特講於內外春秋既存其名而復著其實此可見聖
人內夏外夷之旨矣夫自晉伯不競楚勢復張辰陵
有盟楚莊之竊伯也陳鄭從之猶幸晉人之未從于
蜀有講嬰齊之主盟也列國與之猶幸晉人之不與
迨夫于宋之會爭先晉歃而中國之君分為交見之
從于虢之會仍讀舊書而天下之伯遂成南北之勢
楚人至是益横矣故春秋於辰陵于蜀之盟每先楚
以紀其實于宋于虢之會但先晉以正其名所謂盟

生、鄭罕虎、許人、曹人于虢。〔昭公元年〕公會晉侯及吳子于黄池。〔哀公十三年〕

程宏
同考試官訓導鄭批：塲中作此題者，多昧本旨，間能知之而又不能發。唯此卷經旨詳明，措詞雄健，非熟於《麟經》者不能也。
考試官檢討邢批：《春秋》於內外名實之分甚嚴，此作能發揮之，是可尚也。
考試官脩撰劉批：聖人謹名實之辨，正以內夏外夷，此作得之矣。

盟會迭講於內外，《春秋》始紀其實而終正其名；好會特講於內外，《春秋》既存其名而復著其實。此可見聖人內夏外夷之旨矣。夫自晉伯不競，楚勢復張。辰陵有盟，楚莊之竊伯也，陳、鄭從之，猶幸晉人之未從；于蜀有講，嬰齊之主盟也，列國與之，猶幸晉人之不與。迨夫于宋之會，爭先晉歃，而中國之君分為交見之從；于虢之會，仍讀舊書，而天下之伯遂成南北之勢，楚人至是益横矣。故《春秋》於辰陵、于蜀之盟，每先楚以紀其實；于宋、于虢之會，但先晉以正其名。所謂盟

…Gongsun Guisheng of Cai, Han Hu of Zheng, a man of Xu, and a man of Cao at Guo [First year of Duke Zhao]. The Duke met the Marquis of Jin and the Viscount of Wu at Huangchi [Thirteenth year of Duke Ai].”

Cheng Hong 程宏
Comment by Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Zheng: Among the candidates in the examination hall writing on this topic, most were blind to its fundamental purport; occasionally some understood it yet were unable to bring it out. Only this paper sets forth the meaning of the Classic with detailed clarity and employs vigorous diction—none but one thoroughly versed in the Classic of the Unicorn (Spring and Autumn Annals) could have achieved this.
Comment by Examiner and Examining Editor Xing: The Spring and Autumn Annals is extremely strict regarding the distinction between internal and external, and between name and reality. That this composition is able to expound upon it is commendable.
Comment by Examiner and Senior Compiler Liu: The Sage was scrupulous in distinguishing name and reality precisely in order to treat the Huaxia states as internal and the barbarian tribes as external. This composition has grasped it.

When covenants and meetings were repeatedly negotiated between the internal states and external tribes, the Spring and Autumn Annals first recorded the reality of the situation and in the end rectified their names; when a friendly meeting was specifically negotiated between the internal and the external, the Spring and Autumn Annals both preserved their names and furthermore made manifest the reality. From this one may see the Sage’s purport in treating the Huaxia as internal and the barbarians as external. Now, from the time the hegemon of Jin ceased to be strong, the power of Chu grew arrogant once more. When there was the covenant at Chenling, it was King Zhuang of Chu usurping the hegemony; Chen and Zheng followed him, yet it was still fortunate that the men of Jin did not follow. When there was the negotiation at Shu, it was Yingqi presiding over the covenant; the various states participated in it, yet it was still fortunate that the men of Jin did not participate. By the time of the meeting at Song, Chu contended to smear its lips with blood ahead of Jin, and the rulers of the Central States were divided into followers paying reciprocal court to both; at the meeting at Guo, they read the old covenant text once again, and the hegemony of the realm thereupon formed a posture of north versus south. By this point the men of Chu had grown even more unbridled. Therefore, in the covenants at Chenling and at Shu, the Spring and Autumn Annals in each case placed Chu first so as to record the reality; in the meetings at Song and at Guo, it merely placed Jin first so as to rectify the names. title: 天順六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
萬物之理
胡煦
同考試官教諭周批題本正大人多忽畧或專以樂之效驗為言
或獨以樂之器數為說令人厭觀忽得此
卷詞順理明歆羡歆羡
考試官檢討那批發明君子興和樂以極功用之妙皆本之自
養必深於禮者
考試官脩撰劉批文贍意足可以備選
惟君子能自養以脩其身斯可興和樂而著其用夫
===
和樂由人順氣而興也苟君子無自養之功則身且
不脩又何以著樂之功用哉記樂者謂夫人感於聲
而氣之應者有順有逆則氣成於象而樂之興者有
和有淫是以君子不可無自養之功焉自養何如彼
耳目鼻口四肢百體皆身之運於外者而心則主乎
內者也君子必姦聲亂色不留於聰明飲食臭味不
溺於外誘使耳目鼻口皆由順正而所行一合乎天
理之宜淫樂慝禮不接於心術惰慢邪僻之氣不設
於身體俾心知百體皆由順正而所為不悖乎當然

萬物之理

胡煦
同考試官教諭周批：「題本正大，人多忽畧，或專以樂之效驗為言，或獨以樂之器數為說，令人厭觀。忽得此卷，詞順理明，歆羡歆羡。」
考試官檢討那批：「發明君子興和樂以極功用之妙，皆本之自養，必深於禮者。」
考試官脩撰劉批：「文贍意足，可以備選。」

惟君子能自養以脩其身，斯可興和樂而著其用。夫和樂由人順氣而興也，苟君子無自養之功，則身且不脩，又何以著樂之功用哉？記樂者謂夫人感於聲，而氣之應者有順有逆，則氣成於象，而樂之興者有和有淫，是以君子不可無自養之功焉。自養何如？彼耳目鼻口、四肢百體，皆身之運於外者，而心則主乎內者也。君子必姦聲亂色不留於聰明，飲食臭味不溺於外誘，使耳目鼻口皆由順正，而所行一合乎天理之宜；淫樂慝禮不接於心術，惰慢邪僻之氣不設於身體，俾心知百體皆由順正，而所為不悖乎當然
translation_en:
"[Until the principles of] all things [reached their culmination with the utmost harmony.]"

Hu Xu 胡煦
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Zhou 周: "The topic is inherently upright and grand, yet people mostly overlook it, either speaking exclusively of the efficacy of music or discussing solely the instruments and numerical proportions of music, making them tiresome to read. Suddenly obtaining this paper, with its smooth phrasing and clear reasoning—how admirable, how admirable!"
Comment by Examiner Examining Editor Na 那: "He elucidates how the gentleman gives rise to harmonious music to reach the subtlety of its supreme efficacy, rooting it all in self-cultivation; he must be one deeply versed in the Record of Rites."
Comment by Examiner Senior Compiler Liu 劉: "The writing is rich and the meaning complete; it is worthy of selection."

Only when the gentleman is able to nurture himself so as to cultivate his person can he give rise to harmonious music and manifest its efficacy. Now, harmonious music arises from a person's compliant vital energy (qi). If the gentleman lacks the effort of self-nurturing, then even his own person will go uncultivated—how then could he manifest the efficacy of music? The recorder of the "Record of Music" (Yueji) states that when a person is stirred by sounds, the vital energy that responds may be either compliant or perverse; and when that vital energy takes form in outward phenomena, the music that arises may be either harmonious or licentious. Therefore, the gentleman cannot do without the effort of self-nurturing. What is self-nurturing like? Those ears, eyes, nose, and mouth, and the four limbs and hundred parts of the body, are all what the person operates on the outside, whereas the mind is what presides within. The gentleman must ensure that depraved sounds and disorderly sights do not linger in his hearing and vision, and that food, drink, odors, and flavors do not mire him in external temptations, causing his ears, eyes, nose, and mouth all to follow compliance and rectitude, so that his actions uniformly accord with what is fitting in heavenly principle; he must ensure that licentious music and corrupt rites do not come into contact with the workings of his mind, and that indolent,remiss, perverse, and偏頗 airs are not established in his body, causing his mind, intellect, and the hundred parts of his body all to follow compliance and rectitude, so that what he does does not go against what ought to be…

title: 天順六年應天府鄉試錄
text:
會迭講於內外春秋始紀其實而終正其名者如此
自是厥後晉伯益衰黃池之會吳晉爭長彼吳子以
文身之裔恃戰勝之威稱為周室之長偃然而不怍
爭先中國之盟侈然而不憚彼向也楚雖主盟不過
列國從之而已今則魯哀以秉禮之望亦聽命於號
令之下昔也楚雖先晉不過大夫同之而已今則晉
定以奕世之伯遂俯首於壇坫之間吳勢至此亦張
矣故春秋於黃池之會既先晉以存中國之名復書
及以著兩伯之實所謂好會特講於內外春秋既存
===
其名而復著其實者又如此嗟夫晉之為國天下莫
